title: Quadrupole formula
tagline: How a changing spread of mass sets the size of gravitational waves
aliases: quadrupole formula for the wave field
summary: Two stars circling each other keep changing how their mass is spread out, and not equally in every direction. That changing spread sends out gravitational waves. The quadrupole formula gives the size of those waves far away: the same change made quicker makes bigger waves, and twice as far away the waves are half as big. A perfectly round ball that swells and shrinks evenly sends out none, because its spread changes equally in every direction.

objectives.can_do: Explain why a changing spread of mass, not total mass or motion alone, makes gravitational waves, and pick out moving objects that make none.

Compute the strain and polarizations of a circular binary or a spinning deformed star.
Distinguish the transverse-traceless part of the field, which a detector records, from the rest, including the sign error from the rigid-body inertia tensor.
Explain why a constant mass quadrupole does not mean silence, and estimate when a binary is too fast for the formula.
State the hypotheses of the formula and explain why it holds for slow, wide binaries of neutron stars or black holes.
Prove that the transverse-traceless projector removes any trace, and relate different definitions of the mass moment.
Apply the transverse-traceless projector to find a source's polarizations in any direction, and explain why some directions receive no wave.

ways_in.title: A spinning pair keeps changing its spread
ways_in.question: What about two circling stars makes gravitational waves?
ways_in.explanation:
Lay a pencil flat on a table and spin it about its middle. Picture the same motion in space, with two equal stars in place of the pencil's ends. The stars circle each other around the point midway between them, so the pair spins like the pencil.

A pair like this sends out gravitational waves. A gravitational wave is a ripple that travels outward at the speed of light. Across its direction of travel, it stretches distances along one line while it squeezes them along the line at right angles.

Picture an L of two equal arms, with free-floating mirrors at their ends. Laser light sent along each arm measures its length. When the arms line up with the stretching and squeezing, a passing wave makes one arm longer and the other shorter. The difference between their lengths, as a fraction of one arm's length, is called the strain. A strain of one part in a million would make two arms, each one kilometre long, differ by one millimetre.

A ripple needs something that rises and falls. The pair's total mass does not, so it cannot make one. The pair's balance point is called its centre of mass. Nothing outside pushes on the pair, so its centre of mass stays put or drifts almost perfectly steadily in a fixed direction. A steady drift does not rise and fall either.

What does rise and fall is how the mass is spread out. Draw a line through the centre of mass, lying in the plane where the stars circle. When the stars line up along your line, the mass is spread far along it. A quarter turn later, the stars lie across your line. Each star now sits beside the centre, not out along your line, so the spread along it is zero. After half a turn, the stars line up along your line again. So the spread along your line rises and falls twice for every turn of the pair.

The waves repeat as often as the spread does, twice per turn.

This measure of how far the mass is spread along each direction, around its centre of mass, is called the mass quadrupole.
ways_in.try_it: Draw a line on paper. Hold a pen flat just over the line, with the pen's middle over the line, and turn the pen slowly through one full turn. Count the moments when the pen lies exactly along the line. You should count two, half a turn apart. So the spread along the line peaks twice per turn, and so do the waves.
ways_in.takeaway: A circling pair makes gravitational waves because its spread of mass along a line rises and falls twice per turn.
ways_in.simplifies: Finer details of a shape add much weaker waves that the mass quadrupole leaves out.

ways_in.title: Moving is not enough
ways_in.question: Which moving or changing objects send out no gravitational waves?
ways_in.recap: A gravitational wave stretches distances along one line across its path while it squeezes them along the line at right angles. The mass quadrupole measures how far a source's mass is spread along each direction around its centre. A circling pair sends out waves because its spread along a line rises and falls twice per turn.
ways_in.explanation:
A balloon swells, a wheel spins, a bar tumbles, a square of weights turns. Not all of them send out gravitational waves. What decides is whether the spread of mass changes differently along different directions.

Picture a perfectly round balloon of gas in space that swells and shrinks over and over, staying perfectly round. Its mass spreads farther as it swells, but by the same amount along every direction. A gravitational wave must stretch one line while it squeezes the line at right angles. A change that is the same in every direction picks no line to stretch. So the balloon sends out no gravitational waves, however fast it swells.

A perfectly even wheel, the same all the way around, looks the same at every moment as it spins, so no waves go out. A tumbling bar is different: like the pair, it sends out waves.

A spinning square of four equal weights is a trap. Its two diagonals are like two equal bars crossed at a right angle. As the square turns, one bar's spread along a line rises exactly as much as the other's falls. Check it with weights 1 metre from the centre, adding up squared distances along the line. A diagonal along the line gives 1 plus 1 from its two ends, and 0 from the two weights beside the centre, which is 2. A side along the line puts all four weights about 0.71 metres out. Because 0.71 times 0.71 is about a half, the four also give 2. So the quadrupole formula gives no waves.

Yet after an eighth of a turn the square looks different, so it does send out waves, far weaker ones that the formula leaves out.
ways_in.try_it: Draw a line on paper. Lay a coin and a pencil on it, each with its middle on the line, and the pencil along the line. Give each a quarter turn, flat on the paper, about its middle. The coin covers the line as before, but the pencil now lies across it. Only the pencil's spread along the line changed, so a spinning pencil shape sends out waves and a perfectly even spinning coin does not.
ways_in.takeaway: Motion by itself is not enough. An evenly swelling round balloon or an even spinning wheel sends out no gravitational waves. A tumbling bar or a circling pair does, because its spread changes differently along different directions.
ways_in.simplifies: Real balloons and wheels are never perfectly even, so their small bumps send out extremely weak waves. A perfectly round balloon and a perfectly even wheel send out none at all.

ways_in.title: Faster spin, farther detector
ways_in.question: What happens to the strain with faster spin or a farther detector?
ways_in.recap: A gravitational wave passing two equal arms at right angles, lined up with its stretching and squeezing, makes one longer and the other shorter. The strain is the difference in their lengths, as a fraction of one arm's length. The mass quadrupole measures how far a source's mass is spread along each direction around its centre. A circling pair's spread along a line peaks twice per turn.
ways_in.explanation:
A steel bar spinning flat about its middle has a spread that rises and falls like the pair's.

The quadrupole formula uses the mass quadrupole to find the strain far from a source whose parts move much slower than light. The spread changes at some rate, like a speed. That rate itself keeps changing, the way a car's speed changes as it speeds up and slows down. The strain is set by how fast that rate changes.

Spin the bar twice as fast. Its spread swings as far in half the time, so the rate of change doubles. That doubled rate also rises and falls in half the time, so it changes four times as fast, and the strain grows four times. The same stars can circle faster only by moving closer together, which shrinks their spread, so their strain grows by less.

Twice as far away, the strain is half as big. The wave's energy is shared over a sphere, and a sphere twice as wide has four times the area. So each square metre gets a quarter of the energy. For waves that repeat equally fast, the energy grows as the square of the strain, as a spring stretched twice as far stores four times the energy. So the strain falls to a half.

In 2015, detectors with 4-kilometre arms measured waves from two black holes circling each other more than a billion light-years away. Shortly before the black holes merged, the formula gives a strain of nearly one part in a thousand billion billion, close to the size measured. The black holes were then moving at a third of light speed relative to each other, too fast for more than a rough estimate.

Picture such a bar, 10 metres long with a mass of 10 tonnes, spinning five times per second. Along its spin axis at the Moon's distance, its strain would have forty-four zeros after the decimal point before the first digit. So nobody notices gravitational waves in daily life.
ways_in.takeaway: Faster spinning gives a bigger strain, and twice as far away the strain is half as big.
ways_in.simplifies: The formula needs the source to be much smaller than its wavelength, the distance its waves travel while they repeat once. While a pair's waves repeat once, each star travels half a lap, about the pair's width. In that time the waves travel one wavelength, at light speed. So the source is small enough when the stars move much slower than light. You must also be many wavelengths away. Within about a sixth of a wavelength, the ordinary pull of the moving stars stretches and squeezes more than the waves do. Farther out, that pull fades much faster than the waves.

ways_in.title: From the retarded integral to the formula
ways_in.question: How does the quadrupole formula follow from the linearized field equations, and where does each assumption enter?
ways_in.explanation:
"Faster spin, farther detector" made three claims: the strain follows the second time derivative of how the mass is spread, it falls as $1/r$, and it carries a tiny prefactor. All three come out of the linearized field equations. In Lorenz gauge, with the course conventions, $\Box\bar h_{\mu\nu} = -16\pi G T_{\mu\nu}/c^4$, and the solution with only outgoing waves is the retarded integral

$$\bar h_{\mu\nu}(t,\mathbf x) = \frac{4G}{c^4}\int\frac{T_{\mu\nu}\big(t - |\mathbf x - \mathbf y|/c,\ \mathbf y\big)}{|\mathbf x - \mathbf y|}\,d^3y.$$

Let the source have size $L$ and radiate at wavelength $\lambda$, and put the origin at its centre of mass, a distance $r$ from the field point. Three conditions simplify the integral.

- *Compact source*, $L \ll r$: replace $1/|\mathbf x - \mathbf y|$ by $1/r$, with a relative error of order $L/r$.
- *Slow motion*, $L \ll \lambda$: retarded times across the source differ by at most $L/c$, a small fraction of a period, so evaluate every element at $t - r/c$. Internal speeds are of order $cL/\lambda$, so this is the condition $v \ll c$.
- *Wave zone*, $r \gg \lambda$: not needed for the algebra, but needed to read the result as a wave. Closer in, near-zone fields that fall off faster than $1/r$ are not negligible, inside about $\lambda/2\pi$ they dominate, and the field is not locally a plane wave.

Only the spatial components are needed, because the transverse-traceless part that moves free masses lives in them: $\bar h_{ij} \approx (4G/c^4 r)\int T_{ij}(t - r/c, \mathbf y)\,d^3y$. Stresses inside a source are hard to know, but conservation, $\partial_\nu T^{\mu\nu} = 0$, ties them to the motion of mass. The tensor virial identity gives $\int T^{ij}\,d^3y = \tfrac12\ddot I^{ij}$, where $I^{ij} = \int\rho\,y^iy^j\,d^3y$ is the second mass moment and $\rho = T^{00}/c^2$ at leading order. The entry picture's spread along a line with unit direction $\mathbf u$ is $u_iu_jI_{ij} = \int\rho\,(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf y)^2\,d^3y$, and its rate of change of the rate of change is $u_iu_j\ddot I_{ij}$. So

$$\bar h_{ij}(t,\mathbf x) = \frac{2G}{c^4 r}\,\ddot I_{ij}(t - r/c).$$

Read the result one feature at a time.

- The prefactor $2G/c^4 = 1.65\times10^{-44}\ \mathrm{s^2\,kg^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$ makes every strain small. Writing $\ddot I \sim Mv^2$ for a source of mass $M$ gives $h \sim (GM/rc^2)(v/c)^2$: the source's Newtonian potential at the detector, in units of $c^2$, suppressed by $(v/c)^2$.
- Only the time-varying part of $\ddot I_{ij}$ radiates. Moving the origin adds $MX_iX_j$ for a centre of mass at $\mathbf X$; if $\mathbf X$ moves at constant velocity $\mathbf V$, this adds the constant $2MV_iV_j$ to $\ddot I_{ij}$, a steady field and not a wave.
- A part of $I_{ij}$ proportional to $\delta_{ij}$ cannot stretch one transverse direction against another. The transverse-traceless projection removes it, so the trace-free part of $I_{ij}$ gives the same wave.
- The $1/r$ describes the field. The energy flux, quadratic in the field, falls as $1/r^2$.
ways_in.takeaway: Far from a compact, slowly moving source, conservation turns the retarded integral of the stresses into two G over c to the fourth r, times the second time derivative of the mass moment at the retarded time.
ways_in.simplifies: Assumes linearized gravity and flat-space conservation of the matter's stress-energy. The way "Hypotheses, gauge, and self-gravitating sources" explains why the result survives for sources bound by their own gravity.

ways_in.title: What a distant detector records
ways_in.question: Which strain does a detector far from a circling binary record, and how does it depend on the viewing direction?
ways_in.explanation:
The formula of "From the retarded integral to the formula" hands over six components $\bar h_{ij}$, but a detector responds to only two combinations. Picture a laser interferometer far from the source, with free-hanging end mirrors on two equal arms of length $\ell$ along $x$ and $y$, and a wave arriving along $z$. The arms change length by $+\tfrac12h_+\ell$ and $-\tfrac12h_+\ell$, so the recorded strain, the arm-length difference divided by $\ell$, is $h_+$, where

$$h_+ = \tfrac12\big(\bar h_{xx} - \bar h_{yy}\big),\qquad h_\times = \bar h_{xy}.$$

Arms turned by $45^\circ$ about $z$ record $h_\times$ instead. The components $\bar h_{xz}$, $\bar h_{yz}$ and $\bar h_{zz}$, which carry an index along the line of sight, and the transverse trace $\bar h_{xx} + \bar h_{yy}$ move no mirror relative to another. The transverse-traceless projection removes them.

Now point the detector at a circular binary: masses $m_1$ and $m_2$, total mass $M$, reduced mass $\mu = m_1m_2/M$, separation $a$, and orbital angular frequency $\omega$ with $\omega^2 = GM/a^3$. In the centre-of-mass frame the second mass moment is $I_{ij} = \mu x_ix_j$, with $\mathbf x$ the relative position. The derivation "Polarizations of a circular binary" gives, at inclination $\iota$ between the orbital axis and the line of sight,

$$h_+ = -\tfrac12h_0(1 + \cos^2\iota)\cos 2\omega t_r,\qquad h_\times = -h_0\cos\iota\,\sin 2\omega t_r,\qquad h_0 = \frac{4G\mu a^2\omega^2}{c^4 r} = \frac{4G^2\mu M}{c^4 a r},$$

with $t_r = t - r/c$. A detector reads off four things.

- *Frequency.* The waves oscillate at angular frequency $2\omega$, so their frequency $f = \omega/\pi$ is twice the orbital frequency.
- *Direction.* Face-on, $\iota = 0$, both polarizations have amplitude $h_0$ and are a quarter cycle apart: circular polarization. Edge-on, $\iota = 90^\circ$, only $h_+$ survives, with amplitude $h_0/2$: linear polarization.
- *Distance.* The amplitude falls as $1/r$, so halving a detector's noise doubles its reach and multiplies the volume it surveys by 8.
- *Orbit size.* At fixed masses $h_0 \propto 1/a$, so the signal grows as the orbit shrinks.

For black holes of 36 and 29 solar masses at 410 Mpc, where $1$ Mpc $= 3.086\times10^{22}$ m, the worked example "Strain from a black-hole pair" gives $h_0 \approx 8\times10^{-22}$ when the waves pass 35 Hz, the same order as the peak strain of $1.0\times10^{-21}$ recorded for GW150914. Pulsar timing tests the formula another way: it measures the energy the waves carry off, through the shrinking orbit of a binary pulsar.
ways_in.takeaway: A detector records only the transverse-traceless part of the field; a circular binary sends waves at twice its orbital frequency, circularly polarized face-on and linearly polarized, at half the amplitude, edge-on.
ways_in.simplifies: Treats the orbit as a fixed Newtonian circle over a few cycles and ignores the cosmological redshift, about 9 percent for GW150914.

ways_in.question: Under exactly what hypotheses does the quadrupole formula hold, and why does it apply to binaries bound by their own gravity?

$$h^{\mathrm{TT}}_{ij} =  rac{2}{r}\,\Lambda_{ij,kl}(\mathbf n)\,\ddot I_{kl}(t - r)\, ig[1 + O(v) ig] + O(r^{-2}),$$

where $P_{ij} = \delta_{ij} - n_in_j$ and $\Lambda_{ij,kl} = P_{ik}P_{jl} - 	frac12P_{ij}P_{kl}$ projects symmetric tensors onto their transverse, traceless part. Because $\Lambda_{ij,kl}\delta_{kl} = 0$, the full and the trace-free moment give the same field. The time components at this order follow from the Lorenz condition, $ ar h^{0j} = n_k ar h^{jk}$ and $ ar h^{00} = n_jn_k ar h^{jk}$, apart from non-radiative pieces such as $4M/r$. glossary.plain_definition: A ripple that travels outward at the speed of light. Across its direction of travel, it stretches distances along one line while it squeezes them along the line at right angles.
The size of a gravitational wave's stretching. For two equal arms at right angles, lined up with the stretching and squeezing, it is the difference in their lengths as a fraction of one arm's length.
The balance point of an object or a group of objects. For a pair of equal stars, it is the point midway between them.
A measure of how far an object's mass is spread along each direction around its centre of mass.
The rule that gives the strain far from a slowly moving source, from how fast the rate of change of its mass quadrupole is changing. The strain halves when the distance doubles.
The distance a wave travels while it repeats once.
A region where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can get out.
The distance light travels in one year, about nine and a half million million kilometres.

derivations.title: The quadrupole formula from the retarded integral
derivations.goal: Show that far from a compact, slowly moving source with conserved stress-energy, $\bar h_{ij} = (2G/c^4 r)\,\ddot I_{ij}(t - r/c)$.
steps:
In Lorenz gauge the course conventions give $\Box ar h_{\mu
u} = -16\pi G T_{\mu
u}/c^4$, whose outgoing solution is $ ar h_{\mu
u}(t,\mathbf x) = (4G/c^4)\int T_{\mu
u}(t - |\mathbf x - \mathbf y|/c,\mathbf y)\,|\mathbf x - \mathbf y|^{-1}\,d^3y$.

Check the sign with the static limit: for matter at rest $T_{00} = \rho c^2$, so $\bar h_{00} = (4G/c^2)\int\rho\,|\mathbf x - \mathbf y|^{-1}d^3y = -4\Phi/c^2$, and trace reversal gives $h_{00} = -2\Phi/c^2$, the Newtonian limit $g_{00} = -(1 + 2\Phi/c^2)$.
Compact source: for $|\mathbf y| \le L \ll r$, $|\mathbf x - \mathbf y| = r - \mathbf n\cdot\mathbf y + O(L^2/r)$. In the denominator keep only $r$.
Slow motion: in the time argument the shift $\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf y/c$ is at most $L/c$, a small fraction of a period when $L \ll \lambda$. Drop it, so every element is evaluated at $t_r = t - r/c$.
The spatial components become $\bar h_{ij} = (4G/c^4 r)\int T_{ij}(t_r,\mathbf y)\,d^3y$.

With $x^0 = ct$, conservation reads $\partial_0T^{00} + \partial_kT^{k0} = 0$ and $\partial_0T^{0j} + \partial_kT^{kj} = 0$. Differentiate the first with respect to $x^0$ and use the second: $\partial_0^2T^{00} = \partial_j\partial_kT^{jk}$.

Multiply by $y^ly^m$ and integrate over a region containing the source. Two integrations by parts, with no boundary terms because $T^{\mu\nu}$ vanishes outside, give $\int y^ly^m\,\partial_j\partial_kT^{jk}\,d^3y = \int\partial_j\partial_k(y^ly^m)\,T^{jk}\,d^3y$.
$\partial_j\partial_k(y^ly^m) = \delta^l_j\delta^m_k + \delta^m_j\delta^l_k$, and $T^{jk}$ is symmetric, so the right side is $2\int T^{lm}\,d^3y$.

The left side is $\partial_0^2\int T^{00}y^ly^m\,d^3y$ with $\partial_0^2 = c^{-2}\partial_t^2$. At leading order in $v/c$, $T^{00} = \rho c^2$, so it equals $\ddot I^{lm}$ with $I^{lm} = \int\rho\,y^ly^m\,d^3y$.
So $\int T^{lm}\,d^3y = \tfrac12\ddot I^{lm}$, the tensor virial identity.
Substitute into the spatial components and lower indices with $\delta_{ij}$: $\bar h_{ij}(t,\mathbf x) = (2G/c^4 r)\,\ddot I_{ij}(t - r/c)$.

Where $r \gg \lambda$ the field is locally a plane wave along $\mathbf n$, and free masses respond only to its transverse-traceless part, $h^{\mathrm{TT}}_{ij} = \Lambda_{ij,kl}(\mathbf n)\bar h_{kl}$ with $\Lambda_{ij,kl} = P_{ik}P_{jl} - \tfrac12P_{ij}P_{kl}$ and $P_{ij} = \delta_{ij} - n_in_j$.
derivations.result: $\bar h_{ij}(t,\mathbf x) = \dfrac{2G}{c^4 r}\,\ddot I_{ij}(t - r/c)$ and $h^{\mathrm{TT}}_{ij} = \dfrac{2G}{c^4 r}\,\Lambda_{ij,kl}\ddot I_{kl}(t - r/c)$, with relative corrections of order $L/r$ and $v/c$.

derivations.title: Polarizations of a circular binary
derivations.goal: Find $h_+$ and $h_\times$ for a circular binary seen at inclination $\iota$.
steps: Put the orbit in the $xy$ plane, counterclockwise seen from $+z$, with the centre of mass at the origin. The relative position is $\mathbf x = a(\cos\omega t, \sin\omega t, 0)$, and the bodies sit at $(m_2/M)\mathbf x$ and $-(m_1/M)\mathbf x$.
Then $I_{ij} = \big[m_1(m_2/M)^2 + m_2(m_1/M)^2\big]x_ix_j = \mu x_ix_j$.

With double-angle identities, $I_{xx} = \tfrac12\mu a^2(1 + \cos 2\omega t)$, $I_{yy} = \tfrac12\mu a^2(1 - \cos 2\omega t)$ and $I_{xy} = \tfrac12\mu a^2\sin 2\omega t$; every component with a $z$ index vanishes.
Differentiate twice: $\ddot I_{xx} = -2\mu a^2\omega^2\cos 2\omega t$, $\ddot I_{yy} = +2\mu a^2\omega^2\cos 2\omega t$, $\ddot I_{xy} = -2\mu a^2\omega^2\sin 2\omega t$.

Take the line of sight $\mathbf n = (\sin\iota, 0, \cos\iota)$ and transverse unit vectors $\mathbf p = (\cos\iota, 0, -\sin\iota)$ and $\mathbf q = (0,1,0)$, so that $(\mathbf p, \mathbf q, \mathbf n)$ is right-handed.

The polarization tensors $e^+_{ij} = p_ip_j - q_iq_j$ and $e^\times_{ij} = p_iq_j + q_ip_j$ are transverse and traceless, with $e^+_{ij}e^+_{ij} = e^\times_{ij}e^\times_{ij} = 2$. Contracting with them picks out the transverse-traceless part, so $h_+ = \tfrac12e^+_{ij}\bar h_{ij}$ and $h_\times = \tfrac12e^\times_{ij}\bar h_{ij}$.
Because $\ddot I_{xz} = \ddot I_{zz} = 0$, $e^+_{ij}\ddot I_{ij} = \cos^2\iota\,\ddot I_{xx} - \ddot I_{yy} = -2\mu a^2\omega^2(1 + \cos^2\iota)\cos 2\omega t$.
Likewise $e^\times_{ij}\ddot I_{ij} = 2\cos\iota\,\ddot I_{xy} = -4\mu a^2\omega^2\cos\iota\,\sin 2\omega t$.

Multiply by $\tfrac12\cdot 2G/(c^4 r)$ and evaluate at $t_r = t - r/c$: $h_+ = -\tfrac12h_0(1 + \cos^2\iota)\cos 2\omega t_r$ and $h_\times = -h_0\cos\iota\,\sin 2\omega t_r$, with $h_0 = 4G\mu a^2\omega^2/(c^4 r)$.
Kepler's third law, $\omega^2 = GM/a^3$, turns $h_0$ into $4G^2\mu M/(c^4 a r)$.
derivations.result: $h_+ = -\tfrac12h_0(1+\cos^2\iota)\cos 2\omega t_r$ and $h_\times = -h_0\cos\iota\,\sin 2\omega t_r$: circular polarization face-on, linear polarization with amplitude $h_0/2$ edge-on.

worked_examples.title: Strain from a black-hole pair
worked_examples.problem: Two black holes of $36\,M_\odot$ and $29\,M_\odot$ ($M_\odot = 1.989\times10^{30}$ kg) circle each other 410 Mpc away ($1$ Mpc $= 3.086\times10^{22}$ m). Treating the orbit as a Newtonian circle and ignoring redshift, estimate the face-on strain amplitude when their waves have frequency 35 Hz.
steps: The wave frequency is twice the orbital frequency, so $\omega = \pi f = 110.0$ rad/s.
Kepler's third law gives $a = (GM/\omega^2)^{1/3} = 8.94\times10^5$ m, about 894 km.
worked_examples.answer: $h_0 \approx 8\times10^{-22}$, at a separation of about 894 km.
worked_examples.takeaway: A pair of stellar-mass black holes more than a billion light-years away gives a strain near $10^{-21}$, the size recorded for GW150914, although by then the orbit is fast enough that corrections to the formula matter.

problems.statement: Which of these send out gravitational waves? (a) A perfectly even wheel spinning on its axle. (b) A peanut-shaped rock tumbling end over end in space. (c) A perfectly round balloon of gas that swells and shrinks evenly. (d) Two stars circling each other.
hints: For each one, draw a line through its middle. Does the spread of mass along that line rise and fall?
A gravitational wave must stretch one line while it squeezes the line at right angles.
problems.answer: The tumbling rock and the circling stars send out gravitational waves. The spinning wheel and the swelling balloon send out none.
key_points: The rock and the pair of stars send out waves
The even wheel looks the same at every moment
The round balloon changes equally in every direction
solution: The even wheel looks the same at every moment, so its spread along every line stays the same: no waves.
The rock is longer one way than the other. As it tumbles, its spread along a line through its middle, in the plane where its ends travel, rises and falls twice per turn: waves.
The balloon changes equally along every direction, giving a wave no line to stretch: no waves.
The two stars line up along a line in their plane twice per turn, so the spread along it rises and falls: waves.

problems.statement: A uniform steel rod of mass $1.0\times10^4$ kg and length 10 m spins at 5 revolutions per second about an axis through its centre, perpendicular to the rod. Estimate the strain amplitude along the spin axis at the Moon's distance, $3.84\times10^8$ m. First check that this distance lies in the wave zone.
problems.statement_spoken: A uniform steel rod of mass ten thousand kilograms and length ten metres spins at five revolutions per second about an axis through its centre, perpendicular to the rod. Estimate the strain amplitude along the spin axis at the Moon's distance, three point eight four times ten to the eight metres. First check that this distance lies in the wave zone.
hints: The rod looks the same after half a turn. What is the wave frequency?
For a thin rod along the unit vector $\mathbf u$, $I_{ij} = (ML^2/12)\,u_iu_j$. Compare it with a binary's $\mu x_ix_j$.
problems.answer: The waves have frequency 10 Hz and wavelength $3.0\times10^4$ km, so the Moon is about 13 wavelengths away, in the wave zone. The amplitude is $h_0 = 4G(ML^2/12)\omega^2/(c^4 r) \approx 7\times10^{-45}$.
key_points: Waves at 10 hertz, twice the spin rate
The Moon is about 13 wavelengths away
The rod acts like a binary with mu a squared replaced by M L squared over twelve
Strain about seven times ten to the minus forty-five
solution: The spin angular frequency is $\omega = 2\pi\times5 = 31.4$ rad/s. The rod looks the same after half a turn, so the waves have frequency 10 Hz.

The wavelength is $\lambda = c/f = 3.00\times10^7$ m. The Moon's distance is $r/\lambda = 12.8$ wavelengths, and the rod is far shorter than $\lambda$, so the wave-zone and slow-motion conditions both hold.
For a thin rod, $I_{ij} = \int_{-L/2}^{L/2}(M/L)\,s^2\,ds\;u_iu_j = (ML^2/12)\,u_iu_j$.
This has the form of a binary's $\mu x_ix_j$ with $\mu a^2$ replaced by $ML^2/12 = 8.33\times10^4$ kg m², so along the spin axis $h_0 = 4G(ML^2/12)\omega^2/(c^4 r)$.

problems.statement: A neutron star spins at $f_{\rm s} = 100$ Hz about its body $z$ axis, which points at a detector 1 kpc away ($1$ kpc $= 3.086\times10^{19}$ m). Its rigid-body moments of inertia about the body axes are $J_1$, $J_2$ and $J_3 = 1.0\times10^{38}$ kg m², with $\epsilon = (J_2 - J_1)/J_3 = 1.0\times10^{-6}$. Find the wave frequency and the strain amplitude, taking care to convert moments of inertia into second mass moments.
problems.statement_spoken: A neutron star spins at one hundred hertz about its body z axis, which points at a detector one kiloparsec away. Its rigid-body moments of inertia about the body axes are J one, J two, and J three equal to ten to the thirty-eight kilogram square metres, and J two minus J one divided by J three is one millionth. Find the wave frequency and the strain amplitude, taking care to convert moments of inertia into second mass moments.
hints: In the body frame, $J_2 - J_1 = \int\rho\,(x^2 - y^2)\,d^3y$.
The body-frame difference of the mass moments rotates like a binary's, at twice the spin angular frequency.
problems.answer: The waves have frequency $2f_{\rm s} = 200$ Hz and amplitude $h_0 = 4G\Omega^2\epsilon J_3/(c^4 r) \approx 4.2\times10^{-26}$, with $\Omega = 2\pi f_{\rm s}$, circularly polarized along the spin axis.
key_points: J two minus J one equals the body-frame difference of mass moments
Waves at twice the spin frequency, 200 hertz
Strain about four times ten to the minus twenty-six
solution: $J_1 = \int\rho(y^2 + z^2)$ and $J_2 = \int\rho(x^2 + z^2)$, so $J_2 - J_1 = \int\rho(x^2 - y^2) = I_{xx} - I_{yy}$ in the body frame, and $I_{xy} = 0$ there for principal axes.
Rotating at $\Omega = 2\pi f_{\rm s}$, the detector-frame moments are $I_{xx} - I_{yy} = \epsilon J_3\cos 2\Omega t$ and $I_{xy} = \tfrac12\epsilon J_3\sin 2\Omega t$, plus constants.
Along $z$, $h_+ = \tfrac12(\bar h_{xx} - \bar h_{yy}) = (G/c^4 r)(\ddot I_{xx} - \ddot I_{yy}) = -(4G\Omega^2\epsilon J_3/c^4 r)\cos 2\Omega t_r$.
$h_\times = \bar h_{xy} = (2G/c^4 r)\ddot I_{xy} = -(4G\Omega^2\epsilon J_3/c^4 r)\sin 2\Omega t_r$: circular polarization at $2f_{\rm s} = 200$ Hz.
Using the full tensor $J_{ij}$ in place of $I_{ij}$ would flip the sign of the wave; only the difference $J_2 - J_1$ carries over directly.

problems.statement: Let $\mathbf n$ be a unit vector, $P_{ij} = \delta_{ij} - n_in_j$, and $\Lambda_{ij,kl} = P_{ik}P_{jl} - \tfrac12P_{ij}P_{kl}$. Show that (a) $\Lambda_{ij,kl}\delta_{kl} = 0$; (b) for symmetric $X_{kl}$, $\Lambda_{ij,kl}X_{kl}$ is transverse and traceless; (c) $\Lambda_{ij,mn}\Lambda_{mn,kl} = \Lambda_{ij,kl}$. Conclude which versions of the mass moment give the same wave.
problems.statement_spoken: Let n be a unit vector, P i j the projector transverse to n, and Lambda the product of two P projectors minus one half P i j P k l. Show that Lambda annihilates the identity, that Lambda acting on any symmetric tensor gives a transverse traceless tensor, and that applying Lambda twice is the same as applying it once. Conclude which versions of the mass moment give the same wave.
hints: First show that $P_{ik}P_{kj} = P_{ij}$, $P_{ii} = 2$ and $n_iP_{ij} = 0$.
problems.answer: All three follow from $P^2 = P$, $\mathrm{tr}\,P = 2$ and $P\mathbf n = 0$. So $I_{ij}$ and its trace-free part give the same $h^{\mathrm{TT}}$, a moment defined as three times the trace-free part needs the prefactor divided by 3, and the rigid-body inertia tensor $J_{ij} = I_{kk}\delta_{ij} - I_{ij}$ gives the same wave with the opposite sign.
key_points: P squared is P, its trace is two, and it annihilates n
Lambda annihilates the identity and outputs transverse traceless tensors
Lambda is a projector
Adding a trace leaves the wave unchanged; the rigid-body tensor flips its sign
solution: $P_{ik}P_{kj} = \delta_{ij} - 2n_in_j + n_in_j(n_kn_k) = P_{ij}$, $P_{ii} = 3 - 1 = 2$, and $n_iP_{ij} = n_j - n_j = 0$.
(a) $\Lambda_{ij,kl}\delta_{kl} = P_{ik}P_{jk} - \tfrac12P_{ij}P_{kk} = P_{ij} - P_{ij} = 0$.

(b) Every term of $n_i\Lambda_{ij,kl}$ contains $n_iP_{ik}$ or $n_iP_{ij}$, both zero, so the result is transverse. Its trace is $P_{ik}P_{il}X_{kl} - \tfrac12P_{ii}P_{kl}X_{kl} = P_{kl}X_{kl} - P_{kl}X_{kl} = 0$.

(c) Expanding the product, $P_{im}P_{jn}P_{mk}P_{nl} = P_{ik}P_{jl}$; each of the two cross terms gives $-\tfrac12P_{ij}P_{kl}$; and $\tfrac14P_{ij}P_{mn}P_{mn}P_{kl} = \tfrac12P_{ij}P_{kl}$. The sum is $\Lambda_{ij,kl}$.

By (a), adding any multiple of $\delta_{kl}$ to $I_{kl}$ leaves $h^{\mathrm{TT}}$ unchanged, so the full and trace-free moments agree. A moment three times as large needs a prefactor three times smaller. For $J_{kl} = I_{mm}\delta_{kl} - I_{kl}$, (a) gives $\Lambda J = -\Lambda I$.

observations.phenomenon: The shrinking orbit of the binary pulsar PSR B1913+16
observations.connection: Two neutron stars orbit each other every 7.75 hours, and one is a pulsar whose ticks time the orbit precisely. The quadrupole field of the orbit carries energy away, so the orbit shrinks and its period shortens. The measured decay agrees with the rate computed from the quadrupole formula for this eccentric orbit, which confirmed the formula for bodies bound by their own gravity.
observations.numbers: The period shortens by about 76 microseconds per year. The ratio of the measured decay, corrected for the Galaxy's acceleration of the system, to the predicted decay is $0.9983 \pm 0.0016$.

reference.title: Relativistic Measurements from Timing the Binary Pulsar PSR B1913+16

observations.phenomenon: Gravitational waves from the merging black holes of GW150914
observations.connection: The strain rose in frequency from about 35 Hz to 250 Hz before the merger. The quadrupole formula with the inferred masses and distance gives a face-on amplitude of about $8\times10^{-22}$ at 35 Hz, the order of magnitude recorded. The leading-order rise of frequency gave the first estimate of the chirp mass. Near the peak the orbital speed exceeded half the speed of light, and the formula no longer applies there.
observations.numbers: Peak strain $1.0\times10^{-21}$; black holes of about 36 and 29 $M_\odot$; distance about 410 Mpc; chirp mass estimated at about 30 $M_\odot$; about 3 $M_\odot c^2$ radiated.

reference.title: Observation of Gravitational Waves from a Binary Black Hole Merger

teaching_arc.move: Ask how many times the waves repeat per turn, then have the learner turn a pen over a line and count.
teaching_arc.why: Finding the doubled rate fixes attention on the spread of mass.
teaching_arc.predict: For each full turn of the pair, how many times do its waves repeat?

teaching_arc.move: Run the balloon, wheel, tumbling bar and spinning square through the spread test.
teaching_arc.why: Contrast cases break the belief that any motion radiates.
teaching_arc.predict: Does a perfectly round balloon that swells and shrinks send out gravitational waves?

teaching_arc.move: Pose the faster-bar and twice-as-far checks before revealing answers.
teaching_arc.why: Learners often get both scalings wrong.
teaching_arc.predict: Twice as far away, how big is the strain?

teaching_arc.move: Take the retarded integral through each step, then test the wave-zone condition on a nearby sensor.
teaching_arc.why: Learners see which assumption each factor rests on.

teaching_arc.step: Point a detector at a binary
teaching_arc.move: Derive the binary polarizations, compare face-on with edge-on, and estimate a real signal.
teaching_arc.why: It connects the formula to what instruments record.
teaching_arc.predict: Seen from within the plane of the orbit, will both polarizations appear?

teaching_arc.move: State the hypotheses, answer the self-gravitating objection, and locate the breakdown near merger.
teaching_arc.why: It prevents overtrusting the formula at merger and distrusting it for pulsars.

misconceptions.belief: The waves repeat once for each turn of the pair.
misconceptions.why_tempting: A lighthouse with one lamp flashes once per turn.
misconceptions.correction: The pair looks the same after half a turn, so its spread along a line rises and falls twice per turn. The waves follow the spread.

misconceptions.belief: Twice as far away, gravitational waves are four times weaker, like the light from a lamp.
misconceptions.why_tempting: A lamp really does look four times fainter at twice the distance.
misconceptions.correction: Brightness measures energy, which drops to a quarter; the strain measures the size of the stretching, which drops only to a half.

misconceptions.belief: Anything that moves or changes size sends out gravitational waves.
misconceptions.why_tempting: Gravitational waves are often described as ripples from moving masses.
misconceptions.correction: The spread of mass must change differently along different directions. A round balloon swelling evenly, or an even wheel spinning, sends out none.

misconceptions.belief: If the mass quadrupole stays constant, the source sends out no gravitational waves at all.
misconceptions.why_tempting: The formula then gives exactly zero, and it is used so often that it feels exact.
misconceptions.correction: The formula keeps only the leading multipole term. A spinning square of four equal masses radiates weakly through higher moments.

misconceptions.belief: The I in the formula is the moment of inertia tensor from rigid-body mechanics.
misconceptions.why_tempting: Both are built from mass times squared distance and often share a name.
misconceptions.correction: The rigid-body tensor is the trace of the second mass moment times the identity, minus the moment. Using it flips the sign of the wave.

misconceptions.belief: Every component the quadrupole formula gives stretches a detector, including those along the line of sight.
misconceptions.why_tempting: The formula hands over a full three-by-three array.
misconceptions.correction: Only the transverse part with its trace removed moves free masses relative to each other.

misconceptions.belief: The quadrupole formula describes the whole signal of a binary, right through the merger.
misconceptions.why_tempting: It predicts the rising chirp so well that it seems to hold all the way.
misconceptions.correction: It needs speeds much smaller than light, and a black-hole binary passes a third of light speed a few orbits before merger.

misconceptions.belief: The formula comes from weak-field gravity, so it cannot apply to neutron stars or black holes.
misconceptions.why_tempting: Its derivation starts from linearized theory and flat-space conservation.
misconceptions.correction: Exact conservation including gravitational stresses restores the derivation, and internal strong gravity enters only at high post-Newtonian order.

checks.question: Picture a huge, perfectly round balloon of gas far out in space. It swells to twice its width and shrinks back, over and over, and it stays perfectly round the whole time. Does it send out gravitational waves? Why?
checks.answer: No. As the balloon swells, its mass spreads farther, but by the same amount along every direction, because it stays perfectly round. A gravitational wave must stretch one line while it squeezes the line at right angles. A change that is the same in every direction picks no line to stretch. So the balloon sends out no waves, however fast it swells.
key_points: No waves
The spread changes equally in every direction
A wave needs a direction to stretch
hints: Does the spread of mass change more along one direction than along another?

checks.question: A steel bar spins flat about its middle 5 times per second. A detector far away, on the line of the bar's spin axis, measures its gravitational waves. The bar is sped up to 10 times per second, and the detector stays put. How many times per second do the waves now repeat? By how many times does the largest strain grow?
checks.answer: The waves repeat 20 times per second, and the largest strain grows 4 times. The bar looks the same after half a turn. So its spread along a line rises and falls twice per turn, 20 times each second, and the waves repeat as often as the spread. At twice the spin, the spread swings as far in half the time, so its rate of change doubles. That doubled rate also rises and falls in half the time. So it changes 4 times as fast, and the strain grows 4 times.
key_points: Twice per turn gives 20 repeats each second
The rate doubles and repeats twice as often
The strain grows 4 times
hints: After half a turn, does the bar look any different?
What happens to the rate of change of the spread, and to how fast that rate changes?

checks.question: Two detectors measure gravitational waves from the same pair of circling stars. The second detector is twice as far from the stars as the first, in the same direction. How does the largest strain at the second detector compare with that at the first?
checks.answer: Half as big. The waves' energy is shared over a sphere, and a sphere twice as wide has four times the area. So each square metre gets a quarter of the energy. For waves that repeat equally fast, the energy grows as the square of the strain, as for a stretched spring. A quarter of the energy means half the strain, because a half times a half is a quarter.
key_points: Half as big
A quarter of the energy per square metre
Energy grows as the square of the strain
hints: How much more area does a sphere twice as wide have?
If the energy is a quarter, how big is the strain?

checks.question: Four equal masses $m$ sit at the corners of a square, each a distance $s$ from its centre, and the square spins in its own plane about its centre. A student finds $I_{ij}$ constant and concludes that the system emits no gravitational waves at all. Evaluate the claim.
checks.question_spoken: Four equal masses at the corners of a square spin in its plane. A student finds the mass moment constant and concludes there are no gravitational waves at all. Evaluate the claim.
checks.answer: The calculation is right; the conclusion is wrong. With the square in the $xy$ plane, $I_{xx} = I_{yy} = 2ms^2$ and $I_{xy} = 0$ at every angle, so the quadrupole formula gives no field. But it is only the leading multipole term. The square maps to itself after a quarter turn, so fourth-order moments vary at four times the spin rate and radiate, suppressed relative to a quadrupole source of the same size and speed by roughly $(v/c)^2$.
key_points: The formula gives zero
It is only the leading multipole term
Fourth-order moments radiate weakly at four times the spin rate
hints: Add $\cos^2$ over four angles a quarter turn apart.

checks.question: A student uses the rigid-body inertia tensor $J_{ij} = \int\rho\,(|\mathbf y|^2\delta_{ij} - y_iy_j)\,d^3y$ in place of $I_{ij}$ in the quadrupole formula. Does the physical wave change, and how?
checks.question_spoken: A student uses the rigid-body inertia tensor instead of the second mass moment in the quadrupole formula. Does the physical wave change, and how?
checks.answer: Yes, it flips sign. $J_{ij} = I_{kk}\delta_{ij} - I_{ij}$, and the $\delta_{ij}$ term has no transverse-traceless part, so a detector sees $-I_{ij}$. Both polarizations change sign, a half-cycle shift with unchanged amplitude, which is why the error is easy to miss.
key_points: J equals the trace of I times the identity minus I
The identity term has no transverse traceless part
The wave flips sign with the same amplitude
hints: Write $J_{ij}$ in terms of $I_{ij}$ and its trace.

checks.question: A circular binary orbits in the $xy$ plane. A detector sits far away on the $x$ axis, where the quadrupole formula gives nonzero $\bar h_{xx}$, $\bar h_{yy}$ and $\bar h_{xy}$. Which combinations does it record, and how do their amplitudes compare with the face-on amplitude $h_0 = 4G\mu a^2\omega^2/c^4 r$?
checks.question_spoken: A detector sits in the orbital plane of a circular binary. Which field combinations does it record, and how do they compare with the face-on amplitude?
checks.answer: The wave travels along $x$, so components with an $x$ index are removed and only the traceless part in the $yz$ plane acts: $h_+ = \tfrac12(\bar h_{yy} - \bar h_{zz})$ and $h_\times = \bar h_{yz}$. With $\ddot I_{yy} = 2\mu a^2\omega^2\cos 2\omega t$ and $\ddot I_{zz} = \ddot I_{yz} = 0$, $h_+ = (2G\mu a^2\omega^2/c^4 r)\cos 2\omega t_r$ and $h_\times = 0$: linear polarization at amplitude $h_0/2$, with a sign set by the choice of polarization axes.
key_points: Components with an x index are removed
Only plus polarization survives
Its amplitude is half the face-on amplitude
hints: Which plane is transverse to the direction of travel?

checks.question: A circular binary with fixed masses, seen face-on from a fixed distance, spirals inward until its wave frequency has doubled. By what factor has $h_0$ grown? Why is the answer not 4, as for a rigid rod spun twice as fast?
checks.question_spoken: A face-on circular binary spirals in until its wave frequency doubles. By what factor does the strain amplitude grow, and why not four?
checks.answer: Kepler's third law gives $a^2 \propto \omega^{-4/3}$, so $h_0 = 4G\mu a^2\omega^2/(c^4 r) \propto \omega^{2/3}$, and doubling the frequency multiplies $h_0$ by $2^{2/3} = 1.59$. A rigid rod keeps its length, so its amplitude grows as $\omega^2$; a binary orbits faster only by moving closer, which shrinks $a^2$.
key_points: Kepler ties separation to frequency
A factor of 1.59
The orbit shrinks, unlike a rod
hints: Use Kepler's third law to write $a$ in terms of $\omega$.

checks.question: For black holes of $36\,M_\odot$ and $29\,M_\odot$ on a Newtonian circular orbit, estimate the relative orbital speed $v/c$ when the waves have frequency 35 Hz and 250 Hz. What does this say about the quadrupole formula?
checks.question_spoken: For black holes of thirty-six and twenty-nine solar masses, estimate the orbital speed as a fraction of light speed at wave frequencies of thirty-five and two hundred and fifty hertz. What does it say about the formula?
checks.answer: $v = a\omega = (GM\omega)^{1/3}$ with $\omega = \pi f$ and $M = 65\,M_\odot$ gives $v/c \approx 0.33$ at 35 Hz and $0.63$ at 250 Hz, where the Newtonian orbit is unreliable. Corrections grow as powers of $v/c$, so they matter at 35 Hz, and the formula fails near merger, where post-Newtonian expansions and then numerical relativity take over.
key_points: v over c about 0.33 at 35 hertz
About 0.63 at 250 hertz
The formula fails near merger
hints: Combine $v = a\omega$ with $\omega^2 = GM/a^3$.

checks.question: A laboratory places a sensor 100 km from a spinning source whose waves have frequency 100 Hz, and predicts its signal from $\bar h_{ij} = 2G\ddot I_{ij}/(c^4 r)$. Which condition of the derivation fails, and what dominates the sensor's response instead?
checks.question_spoken: A sensor sits one hundred kilometres from a source radiating at one hundred hertz. Which condition of the quadrupole formula fails, and what dominates instead?
checks.answer: The wavelength is $c/f = 3000$ km, so the sensor is deep in the near zone: the wave-zone condition $r \gg \lambda$ fails, even though the compact-source and slow-motion steps can hold. There the Newtonian tidal field of the moving masses dominates, exceeding the radiative one by a factor of order $(\lambda/2\pi r)^4$, several hundred here, and the field is not a plane wave with a transverse-traceless part to extract.
key_points: The wavelength is 3000 kilometres
The wave-zone condition fails
Near-zone Newtonian tidal fields dominate
hints: Compare the distance with the wavelength.

checks.question: In a binary pulsar, two neutron stars with $GM/Rc^2 \approx 0.2$ at their surfaces orbit each other with $v/c \approx 0.0015$. A referee objects that the quadrupole formula assumed weak fields everywhere and $\partial_\nu T^{\mu\nu} = 0$ in flat spacetime, so it cannot apply. Answer the objection.
checks.question_spoken: A referee says the quadrupole formula cannot apply to a binary pulsar, because it assumed weak fields and flat-space conservation. Answer the objection.

With $h^{\mathrm{TT}}_{ij} = (2/r)\Lambda_{ij,kl}\ddot I_{kl}$, $\mathbf p = \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$ and $\mathbf q = \hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$, find $h_+$ and $h_\times$ at polar angle $\theta$, and the amplitude at $\theta = 30^\circ$ divided by that at $\theta = 90^\circ$. checks.answer: Write $\hat{\mathbf z} = \cos\theta\,\mathbf n - \sin\theta\,\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$, so $P_{ik}\hat z_k = -\sin\theta\,\hat\theta_i$ and $P_{kl}\hat z_k\hat z_l = \sin^2\theta$. So $h_+ = (\sin^2\theta/r)\,\ddot I_{zz}(t - r)$ and $h_\times = 0$, as reflection through the plane containing $\hat{\mathbf z}$ and $\mathbf n$ requires. The ratio is $\sin^2 30^\circ = 0.25$. On the axis $\sin\theta = 0$: $\bar h_{zz}$ has both indices along $\mathbf n$, $\Lambda$ removes it, and it moves no free masses relative to each other, so the student is wrong.

common_questions.question: Why are gravitational waves so weak?
common_questions.answer: Gravity is by far the weakest force between everyday objects. The formula also divides by the speed of light four times over. Only huge masses moving at a good fraction of light speed, like black holes about to merge, make waves big enough to measure.

common_questions.question: Does Earth circling the Sun send out gravitational waves?
common_questions.answer: Yes. Earth and the Sun are a circling pair, so their waves repeat twice a year. The waves are extremely weak, because Earth moves at only about one ten-thousandth of light speed, and the strain depends on the square of that fraction.

novice.retell_attempt: Two stars going round each other are like a spinning pencil, and they make gravitational waves, which stretch space one way and squeeze it the other way. It isn't their mass or their drifting along that does it. It's how their mass is spread along a line, which goes up and down twice every turn, so the waves come twice per turn. The formula says the strain depends on how fast the rate of change is changing, which I didn't really get, and somehow a bar spun twice as fast gives four times the strain. I'm not sure whether that's true for the stars too. Twice as far away it's half, not a quarter, because of energy and squares. stumbles.quote: faster changes make bigger waves

stumbles.rewrite: Across its direction of travel, it stretches distances along one line while it squeezes them along the line at right angles.

stumbles.problem: A length change with no measurer: who measures the arms, and how?
stumbles.rewrite: Picture an L of two equal arms, with free-floating mirrors at their ends. Laser light sent along each arm measures its length.

stumbles.quote: The pair's total mass never changes, and something that never changes cannot make a ripple.
stumbles.problem: Not quite true, since the waves slowly carry energy away, and the reader wonders whether a slow steady loss could make a ripple.
stumbles.rewrite: A ripple needs something that rises and falls. The pair's total mass does not, so it cannot make one.

stumbles.quote: That cannot make a ripple either.
stumbles.problem: No reason is given for why a steadily moving centre of mass makes no ripple.
stumbles.rewrite: A steady drift does not rise and fall either.

stumbles.quote: A quarter turn later, the stars lie across your line, and no mass is spread along it.
stumbles.problem: Reread: the mass has not vanished. The reader cannot see what 'along it' means for stars sitting off to the sides.
stumbles.rewrite: A quarter turn later, the stars lie across your line. Each star now sits beside the centre, not out along your line, so the spread along it is zero.

stumbles.quote: This measure of how far the mass is spread along each direction, around its centre of mass, is called the mass quadrupole. The quadrupole formula uses it to give the strain far away.
stumbles.problem: Two new terms in one paragraph.
stumbles.rewrite: Split into two paragraphs, one naming the mass quadrupole and one naming the quadrupole formula.

stumbles.quote: The strain follows how fast the quadrupole's rate of change is itself changing, the way acceleration tells how fast a speed is changing.
stumbles.problem: Reread twice. 'Follows' could mean copies, lags behind, or is proportional to. 'Acceleration' is a physics word the reader does not have.
stumbles.rewrite: The spread changes at some rate, like a speed. That rate itself keeps changing, the way a car's speed changes as it speeds up and slows down. The strain is set by how fast that rate changes.

stumbles.quote: Spin a steel bar twice as fast, and its spread rises and falls in half the time.
stumbles.problem: The bar appears from nowhere in the middle of the pair picture. The first what-if, stars circling twice as fast, has a different answer, because stars circle faster only by moving closer.
stumbles.rewrite: A steel bar spinning flat about its middle has a spread that rises and falls like the pair's. Spin it twice as fast ... The same stars can circle faster only by moving closer together, so their strain grows by less.

stumbles.quote: The rate of change of the spread doubles, and that rate also changes twice as quickly. So the strain grows four times.
stumbles.problem: The step from 'doubles' and 'twice as quickly' to 'four times' is left implicit.
stumbles.rewrite: Its spread swings as far in half the time, so the rate of change doubles. That doubled rate also rises and falls in half the time, so it changes four times as fast, and the strain grows four times.

stumbles.quote: The wave's energy spreads over a sphere with four times the area
stumbles.problem: 'Spread' is already the word for how mass is arranged, so here one word names two ideas.
stumbles.rewrite: The wave's energy is shared over a sphere, and a sphere twice as wide has four times the area.

stumbles.quote: For waves that repeat equally fast, the energy grows as the square of the strain

stumbles.problem: The link between the speed and the roughness is implicit, because the speed condition had not been tied to it.

Axisymmetric spinning wheel: constant quadrupole and no radiation at any order. It broke the formal sentence 'a source whose mass quadrupole is constant still radiates through higher moments'; changed to 'can still radiate'.

Spinning square of four point weights: zero quadrupole wave, nonzero l = 4 moment at four times the spin rate. The entry sentence that it radiates because it looks different after an eighth of a turn is true for this square. As a general rule it is only generic: extended non-radiating rotating distributions can exist, so the note should not promote it to a law.
Stars of fixed mass circling twice as fast: strain grows by 2^(2/3), not 4; the entry now keeps the bar and the pair apart. Confirmed.

Merger recoil: asymmetric black-hole mergers are kicked by the momentum their waves carry, so a centre of mass does not drift exactly steadily. Entry now says 'almost perfectly steadily'; the recoil is beyond the quadrupole order.

Near zone (a detector a fraction of a wavelength away): the entry claim that the ordinary pull dominates closer than many wavelengths was false between about a sixth of a wavelength and a few wavelengths; rewritten.
Non-relativistic limit: h ~ (GM/rc^2)(v/c)^2 vanishes as v/c goes to 0 at fixed potential; static limit of h-bar_00 recovers Newton with the right sign.

Different choice of gauge: h-bar_ij changes, h^TT does not at leading order in the wave zone; gauge terms include a delta_ij part that the projector also removes.
